My first intro to D&D was in 7th grade when I got kicked out of class when my friend showed me a 2nd edition monster manual. We couldn't stop talking and got sent to the hall. That was great for us, we only had the one book, but we spent those 30 minutes just making up a random adventure on the spot without any real knowledge of the rules, dice, or how the game was supposed to be played. I can't remember any details about the adventure except we fought and killed a white dragon in the Ice Kingdom. That was the spark.

My next encounter with the game was begging my mom to buy me the starter set for 3rd edition when it first released. I invited as many friends as I had premade characters for in the boxed set and we ripped that shit all the way to level 2 or 3, whenever it ends, in one night. This was the hook for me, I knew this was going to be something special. I immediately bought the core rule books and read them cover to cover, I became a rules lawyer without even knowing what it was. And so started a lengthy adventuring career for my friends and I. Eventually life gets in the way, and we drifted apart for one reason or another after high school.

We revived 3/4 of our old core group for 5th edition and I think it is pretty unanimous, we all think this is the best edition. I feel like I'm spending so much less time crunching numbers that we can focus on the more important aspects of the game, and speeds up combat quite a bit.

I run a wiki. In fact, I run several, and one of the things I love to do is find someone who needs help and throw them a rope. I also like to recognize good contributions and congratulate the editors who make them, as I figured if people feel needed, they'll be happy and want to contribute more, and making people happy makes me happy because I used to suffer depression, so smiles help me as much as they uplift others

So for all reading this, if someone seems depressed on a forum or wiki, send them a PM or message letting them know you appreciate them. If they need help, throw them a line. Not only might they return the favor, you're showing you can be a better person to others, which only encourages others to do the same.

In short, compassion is how people can be encouraged to get along and be content online, and if you meet them IRL, do much the same there, you'll get the same results.

There's way too much to get into so I'll just mention two things for now: OOXML and .NET. OOXML is a "standard" that was pushed through ISO under dubious circumstances, and is essentially unimplementable. Even Microsoft can't implement it completely. But, it comes about because some governments were making noise about not wanting to have all their official documents and documents with long-term archival needs stored in an unstable, proprietary format. They've been fighting tooth and nail with various bribes and threats ever since then to prevent anyone from using ODF as an official format. Their goal, is of course, to force every government to standardize on Office, therefore making every taxpayer in the world to pay them indirectly no matter what, and directly if they actually need to read a government document.

As for .NET, it's a little more complicated. They like to talk about how .NET is an ISO standard, but that standard only covers some parts of an ancient version of it. There is somethig called a "Patent Promise" which sounds great as long as you don't read it and think about what it says. As mentioned above, Microsoft released the source code for the C# compiler and some of .NET. Great, right? Well, you can't actually do anything with it, because of the Patent Promise. It only applies to "Covered Code" which is that code "necessarily infringing" a patent to implement either the ISO spec or out-of-spec features as documented on MSDN, and only when that code is used to implement .NET. Basically, you can't use it.
